**Maren** (turn 0):
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

**Traveler** (turn 1):
I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

**Maren** (turn 2):
Maren nodded once, as if the order confirmed something she'd already guessed. She tucked the rag into her apron string and reached under the counter with her left hand for a clean bowl.

"Hot, we have. Old Pell's venison stew. People ride two days for it, and most of them say it was worth the saddle sores." She set the bowl on the pass-through to the kitchen and rapped twice on the wood. A grunt came back through the gap, which was as close to *yes* as Pell ever got. "Comes with bread. The bread is yesterday's, but yesterday was a good day."

She turned back and pulled a heavy ledger from beneath the bar, flipping it open to a page covered in her small, even handwriting. A finger ran down the column.

"Room four is free. Window faces the road, so you'll hear the carts at dawn. Room nine is quieter, but the bed has opinions about how you sleep in it." She glanced up. "Two coppers for either. Stew is one more. Ale is half a copper, and it is local and honest. The wine is imported, and it is overpriced, and I would not insult you by pretending otherwise."

She let that sit a moment.

"I'd know. I set the price."

Her dark eyes flicked, briefly and without comment, to the pack at the Traveler's feet, to the way it had been lowered rather than dropped. Then they came back up, level and unbothered.

"If you've something in there you'd rather not keep in a room with a latch a determined child could lift, I have a strongbox in the back. Locked, bolted to the floor, and I hold the only key." She tapped the silver ring on her left thumb against the counter, a small habitual *tick*. "No charge, and no questions. I have found that questions tend to cost more than they are worth."

Behind her, the kitchen door swung open and a bowl of stew slid onto the bar, steam curling up from it, dark gravy and chunks of venison and a thick heel of bread balanced on the rim. Maren nudged it across with her left hand and set a spoon beside it.

"Eat first. Decide the rest after. Nobody ever made a good choice on an empty stomach." She picked her tally sheet back up. "And if you tell me your name, I'll stop calling you *friend*. It is a perfectly good word, but it wears thin by the second night."

**Traveler** (turn 3):
*I nod, appreciating her honesty.* "Room nine sounds... opinionated. I'll take it." *I push the mysterious package a little further under the bar, out of immediate sight.* "No need for the strongbox, thank you. My name is Traveler." *I pick up the spoon and take a bite of the stew, a sigh escaping me.* "Ah, that's good."

**Maren** (turn 4):
Maren wrote something in the ledger, a short line in that same small, even hand, and blotted it with the side of her left wrist.

"Traveler." She said it the way a person tests a coin between their teeth. "Well. That will certainly make it easy to remember what you do for a living."

She closed the ledger and slid it back beneath the bar. It was a moment before one corner of her mouth moved, very slightly, and then went still again, as though it had thought better of it.

"Room nine, then. Top of the stairs, turn left, last door before the window at the end. If the bed creaks when you roll to the right, that is normal. If it creaks when you have not moved at all, that is the floorboard outside, and it means someone is in the hall. I have never had it fixed." She reached back and took an iron key from a row of hooks, each labeled in chalk, and set it on the counter beside the bowl. "I consider it a feature."

She did not look at the pack again. If she had noted that it had been pushed a little further out of sight, nothing in her face said so. She simply picked up a clean mug with her left hand, pulled a measure of ale from the nearest cask without being asked, and set it down next to the stew.

"On the house. First one always is. Pell gets sulky if people eat his stew without something to wash it down. He says it's like listening to a good song with one ear plugged."

From the kitchen came a muffled, indignant sound that might have been a denial.

"He also says that is not what he said," Maren added, without turning around.

She went back to the tally sheet, running her finger down the column of the evening's orders. In the corner, the grain merchants had lowered their voices further. It was not the hush of men who had settled something. It was the hush of men who were about to disagree more loudly. Maren's eyes lifted to them briefly, measured the distance between one man's hand and his cup, and returned to her figures.

"If you need anything tonight, Traveler, I am down here until well past midnight. Hot water can be brought up for another copper, though I would give Tamsin a few minutes' warning. She is fast, but she is not a miracle, and the kettle is older than she is." She made a small tick on the sheet. "And if anyone comes asking after a road-dusted person carrying something they are being careful with, I will tell them what I tell everybody."

She looked up, level and calm.

"That I run a tavern, not a gossip house, and that the stew is very good tonight."

**Traveler** (turn 5):
A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

**Maren** (turn 6):
Maren looked at the plate the way she might look at a letter delivered to the wrong address.

Four crab cakes, golden and crisp at the edges, arranged in a neat fan on a good pewter plate that had not come from her kitchen. A sprig of something green on top. The smell of butter and brine drifted up and settled over the rosemary of the stew.

She did not reach for it. Her left hand, which had been resting on the counter near the tally sheet, drew back an inch and a half and found the rag at her apron string instead.

"That is very kind of his lordship," she said to the merchant's man, in the same even tone she used for everyone. "Please tell Lord Havel that the Antler thanks him."

Then, with the folded rag between her fingers and the pewter, she slid the plate a careful hand's width down the bar, away from her own side and toward the Traveler's. She did it without hurry, the way she might straighten a crooked candle. She tucked the rag back into her apron string and did not use it again. A moment later she took a fresh one from beneath the counter.

"I do not care for seafood," she said to no one in particular. "Never have. A failing in a tavern keeper, I am told, but I have learned to live with the shame." She paused. "Mostly by not eating seafood."

She turned her head, just slightly, toward the corner table.

It was the louder of the two grain merchants, the one whose hand kept wandering toward his cup. Lord Havel, then. He had the look of a man who owned three good coats and made sure you saw at least two of them. He raised his cup a quarter inch in her direction. Maren inclined her head a quarter inch back, which was exactly the courtesy she would have given a tinker, and not a hair more.

When she spoke again she kept her voice low, meant for the bar and not the room.

"Crab from the coast, arrived this morning," she said. "The coast is three days' ride from here, Traveler, and it has been warm." She picked up her tally sheet with her left hand and ran her eyes down it as though that were the important thing. "I will not tell you what to eat. It is your supper and your stomach. But I have run this place for a long while, and I have noticed that noblemen do not generally send gifts to strangers who have just walked in off the road. Not unless they want to be remembered. Or they want to talk to that stranger. Or they want to know what is in their pack."

She made a small tick on the sheet.

"Possibly all three. He is an ambitious sort of man."

The kitchen door creaked. Tamsin put her head through, a thin girl of perhaps sixteen with flour on one cheek, and caught Maren's eye. Maren tipped her chin toward the stairs, then held up one finger: *room nine, hot water, not yet.* Tamsin nodded and vanished.

Maren set the tally sheet down and rested both forearms on the bar, her left hand on top.

"If you would like to send a thank-you back to his lordship, I can carry it. If you would rather he did not get a closer look at you tonight, I can tell him you were very grateful and very tired, and that you went up early." The corner of her mouth did not move this time. "Both would be true, near enough. I do try to keep my lies close to the truth. It saves wear on the memory."

She glanced once, briefly, at the crab cakes, and then away again, as though they were a dog she did not wish to encourage.

"And if you are finished with that plate, whichever way you decide, leave it where it is. Tamsin will clear it." She tapped her silver ring against the wood, a small *tick*. "I would rather not have his lordship's pewter get mixed up with mine. It is nicer than mine, and I would hate for it to get ideas."

**Traveler** (turn 7):
*I eye the crab cakes. They do look good, despite the warning.* "Hmm. Well, I'm certainly tired." *I push the plate back towards her slightly, away from my own stew.* "Tell him I appreciate the thought, but I'm quite content with Pell's excellent stew tonight. And I'm heading up now." *I grab the key for room nine and finish a mouthful of stew.* "This really is good."

**Maren** (turn 8):
The plate came to rest a few inches from Maren's side of the bar, close enough that the smell of butter and brine rose right up at her.

She did not flinch. She did not look down. She simply took one unhurried step to her left, toward the ale casks, as though she had meant to go there all along, and picked up a clean mug she had no particular use for.

"Very wise," she said. "Pell will be insufferable about it, of course. He'll hear that a man turned down coastal crab for his stew and I'll not get a civil word out of him until the harvest festival." She turned the empty mug over in her left hand and set it back down. "I shall bear it somehow."

She raised two fingers toward the kitchen door without turning her head. Tamsin appeared as if she had been waiting just behind it, which she likely had.

"Tamsin. His lordship's plate, please. Back to his table, with the Antler's thanks and the Traveler's. The Traveler was very grateful and very tired." A pause. "Both true. Mind you use both hands. It's good pewter."

Tamsin took up the plate, crab cakes and all, and carried it across the common room. Maren watched it go. Only when it was a full table's length away did her shoulders ease, a very small movement, the kind no one would see unless they had been watching for it. She took the fresh rag from beneath the counter and wiped down the stretch of bar where the plate had been. Then she wiped it a second time.

"Pewter leaves marks," she said, by way of explanation.

At the corner table, Lord Havel received his plate back with a smile that stayed on his face a moment longer than it wanted to. His eyes went to the bar, to the Traveler, to the empty space on the floor beneath the stool where a pack had been set down so carefully. Then they returned to his companion and his grain prices, and he laughed at something that had not been very funny.

Maren leaned her forearms on the bar again, left hand on top, and spoke low.

"He will ask me about you before the night is out. Men like that always come to the bar eventually. They think they're being clever by waiting." She folded the rag into a neat square. "I'll tell him you paid in honest coin, praised the stew, and went to bed. If he wants more than that, he can buy a room and listen at walls like everyone else. They're thin in places, but not in nine. I saw to that."

She glanced at the iron key in the Traveler's hand, then up again.

"Tamsin will bring your water in a quarter hour. She will knock twice, pause, and knock once more. If anyone knocks any other way, you are under no obligation to open the door." The corner of her mouth moved, just barely. "You're under no obligation to open it for Tamsin either, but then you'll have cold water and she'll have sore arms, and nobody will be happy."

She straightened and picked up her tally sheet.

"The stew is good. I'll tell Pell you said so. It won't improve his temper, but it'll improve mine." Her pen ticked against the page. "Sleep well, Traveler. Mind the bed. It means no harm."

**Traveler** (turn 9):
"Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

**Maren** (turn 10):
Maren's eyebrow, the one with the thin scar through it, rose a fraction of an inch at the first word. Then it settled again, the way a dog lifts its head at a noise and decides the noise is not worth getting up for.

"*Best in months*," she repeated. "I will tell him that part. I will leave the other part out. Pell is a delicate flower where language is concerned. Though not, I have found, where his own language is concerned."

She reached for the nearest cask with her left hand and drew a short measure into a small clay cup, the kind she kept for tasting a new barrel. She did not usually drink behind the bar before the late hours. She lifted it anyway.

"To Old Pell," she said, and turned toward the pass-through. "Pell. You are being toasted. Try to bear it with dignity."

There was a pause from the kitchen. Then came the clang of a ladle set down harder than necessary and a grunt that was, if one had worked with the man for nineteen years, unmistakably pleased.

"He says thank you," Maren translated. "He also says the rosemary was fresh this morning and nobody ever notices the rosemary." She drank. "I noticed the rosemary. I am not permitted to count. Apparently I am *biased*."

She set the cup down and turned her right wrist over, idly, as though easing the old stiffness out of it. For a moment her thumb pressed at a spot just below the heel of her hand, where the skin had begun to look faintly raised. She considered it the way she considered a tally that did not add up. Then she pulled her sleeve down half an inch over it and went on as though nothing had happened.

Across the room, Lord Havel had pushed his chair back. He had not stood yet. He had only pushed it back, the way men do when they are working up to a casual stroll that they have been planning for twenty minutes.

Maren saw it without looking directly at it.

"If you are going up, Traveler, now would be a fine time," she said quietly, picking up her rag. "His lordship has discovered a sudden thirst, and I suspect it is the sort that only conversation will cure." She wiped a spotless stretch of bar. "I will pour him a very slow ale. I am told I am terribly slow at pouring when I am tired. Nobody has ever complained. Or if they did, they did not do it twice."

Her left hand found the oak cudgel's handle beneath the counter. She did not draw it. She only rested her fingers there for a moment, the way someone else might touch a rosary. Then she let go.

"Goodnight, Traveler. Mind the stairs. The third one squeaks, but only for strangers."

**Traveler** (turn 11):
*I chuckle, finishing the last of my ale.* "Goodnight, Maren. And thanks again." *I pick up my pack, careful to keep it close, and head for the stairs. I make sure to step firmly on the third step, just to test the squeak.*

**Maren** (turn 12):
The third stair squeaked. It was a long, complaining note, like a hinge that had been asked one question too many.

Maren did not look up from her rag. "Only for strangers," she said to the bar. The corner of her mouth moved, and this time it stayed moved for nearly a full second before it thought better of it.

Footsteps went on up, and a door opened and shut somewhere on the left side of the landing. Maren listened for the latch, heard it drop, and set her rag down.

Lord Havel arrived at the bar a respectable twenty heartbeats later. He had timed his stroll so that it would look as though he had not been waiting for anyone to leave. He leaned an elbow on the counter, which Maren had just wiped, and smiled at her the way a man smiles at a horse he is thinking of buying.

"Mistress Maren. A splendid house you keep."

"Thank you, my lord. What may I bring you?"

"Oh, an ale. Whatever's local." He waved a hand heavy with rings. "I confess I was hoping for a word with your guest. I seem to have missed my chance."

"You have, my lord." Maren took a mug down with her left hand and turned toward the cask. She set the mug beneath the tap and opened it perhaps a third of the way. The ale came out in a thin amber thread. "The Traveler was very grateful for your kindness and very tired. Paid in honest coin, praised the stew, and went to bed."

"Traveler." Havel chuckled. "Is that a name?"

"It is the one I was given. I have found it answers when called." The thread of ale went on. Havel watched it. Maren watched it too, with the serene attention of a woman who had nowhere else to be until spring.

"Where did they come from, do you suppose? The east road, or the south?"

"I do not suppose, my lord. It is bad for business." She tilted the mug a careful degree. "People who come to the Antler come for the stew and the beds. If they wanted to be supposed about, there is a very good gossip in Harrowby who charges by the hour, and I am told she is worth every copper."

Havel's smile held, but it had to work at it. He reached into his coat, the second-best of the three, and set a silver piece on the counter between them. It rang softly against the wood.

"For your trouble. And perhaps for a little less discretion."

Maren looked at the coin. Then she closed the tap, wiped the base of the mug, and set it down beside the silver without touching the silver at all.

"The ale is half a copper, my lord. I have no change for silver this late, so it is on the house. For your earlier kindness." She met his eyes, level and pleasant. "My discretion is not for sale. I tried selling it once, years ago, and found it was a great deal more expensive to buy back."

For a moment the two of them simply regarded one another across the bar. In the corner, the dwarf turned a page of his letter. In the kitchen, a pot lid rattled.

Havel picked up his silver and tucked it away. He took up the ale instead and sipped it. His face said he had expected worse and was faintly annoyed not to have found it.

"Then I suppose I shall have to take a room," he said lightly, "and make the Traveler's acquaintance at breakfast. You do have rooms, I trust? Something upstairs. On the left, perhaps. I prefer the left."

"We have rooms." Maren drew the ledger from beneath the counter and opened it. Her finger ran down the column with no hurry at all. "Room four is free. On the right, over the road. You will hear the carts at dawn, my lord, which I am told is a great comfort to men of commerce. It reminds them that the world is still buying things."

"Nothing on the left?"

"Nothing on the left that I would put a lord in." She wrote *Havel, 4* in her small, even hand and blotted it with the side of her left wrist. "Two coppers. Breakfast is at first bell. Pell does eggs, if the hens are in a charitable mood."

She took the key to four down from its hook and laid it on the counter. Havel paid in coppers this time. He took the key and his ale and went back to his corner, where the other grain merchant greeted him with the carefully blank expression of a man who had just watched someone lose a small argument.

Maren closed the ledger.

Only then did she turn her back to the room and push her right sleeve up an inch. The raised patch below the heel of her hand had spread into three red welts, each the size of a thumbprint, and they had begun to itch in earnest. She regarded them with mild disapproval.

"Oh, for the love of every saint who ever sat on a thistle," she murmured. It was hardly louder than breathing.

She drew a basin of cold water from the jug beneath the bar and put her wrist in it. She held it there, perfectly still, with her face turned toward the casks as though she were considering which to tap next. After a count of fifty she dried her wrist, rolled the sleeve down, and buttoned the cuff. From a small tin on the shelf, the one labeled *CLOVES* in her own hand, she took a pinch of dried herb that was not cloves. She tucked it into her cheek.

When Tamsin came back through the kitchen door, kettle steaming in both hands, Maren was wiping the bar with her left hand as though nothing in the world had happened.

"Nine," Maren said. "Two knocks, a pause, one knock." Then, more quietly: "And Tamsin. Lord Havel is in four. If you hear the floorboard outside nine tonight, you do not go and look. You come and fetch me."

Tamsin's eyes widened a little, then she nodded and went up. The third stair did not squeak for her at all.

Maren glanced at the candle-clock on the shelf behind the bar. It had burned a little past the tenth mark. Two hours yet. She set out two clean cups at the far end of the bar, side by side, and did not fill them.

Then she went back to her tally sheet, and ran her finger down the evening's orders. One of the numbers no longer added up, and it had nothing at all to do with coin.

**Traveler** (turn 13):
The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

**Maren** (turn 14):
The candle-clock burned down to its twelfth mark just as the bell in the corner gave its first low note. Maren had been watching it, the way she watched it every night.

The common room had emptied an hour ago. The grain merchants had gone up grumbling, Lord Havel's door had shut on the right side of the landing, and the dwarf had folded his letter into his coat and left without a word, which Maren appreciated in a man. Pell had banked the kitchen fire and gone to his cot behind the larder. Only the embers in the hearth and a single lamp on the bar were still lit, and the Traveler, who had come back down some time after the water had gone up. Sleep had evidently lost the argument.

Maren had not asked why. She had only poured a second cup of ale and said, "The bed has opinions. I did warn you."

Now she set down her rag.

On the second note of the bell, she reached beneath the counter with her left hand and brought out a bottle that was not the local ale and not the overpriced wine. It was dark glass, stoppered with wax, and half empty. She broke the seal with her thumbnail as if she had done it a great many times, which she had, from a great many bottles exactly like it.

She filled the first of the two clean cups at the end of the bar. Then the second. She did it slowly and evenly, and the cups came out level to the same hair's breadth.

On the sixth note she picked up one cup and carried the other to the far end of the bar, the end nearest the hearth, where the wood was worn paler than anywhere else. She set it down there. She turned it a quarter turn so the chipped side faced the wall.

The bell struck the last of its twelve and went quiet.

Maren came back to her place across from the Traveler and stood with her cup in her left hand. For a moment she did not drink. She looked at the cup at the end of the bar, not sadly, but the way a person looks at a chair that someone has only just stood up from.

Then she drank, one swallow, and set her cup down.

"It is late, Traveler," she said. Her voice was the same as ever, quiet and level. If anything it was a shade warmer. "Later than most people stay down here. The ones who do usually have something on their mind, or something in their pack, or a bed that talks back. Sometimes all three."

She glanced at the pack. She had noticed it came back down with its owner. Then she looked away again.

"I'll not ask which." She turned her cup a little on the wood. "That's the arrangement here. You don't ask me about my business, I don't ask about yours, and the stew stays good."

She rolled her right cuff back an inch without seeming to think about it. The welts had faded to faint pink shadows, nearly gone. She regarded them, found them satisfactory, and buttoned the cuff again.

Above them a board creaked. It was not the one outside nine. It was further along, on the right, where the floor sagged a little toward the stairwell. Maren lifted her eyes to the ceiling and held them there for the space of three breaths. Nothing else came. She lowered them.

"His lordship is a restless sleeper," she said mildly. "Or a restless something." She picked up the dark bottle and pressed the stopper back in with the heel of her left hand. "Room four is directly over the cellar stair. He'll find the floor there has a great deal to say about anyone who walks on it. I did tell him about the carts. I neglected to mention the floor. It must have slipped my mind."

She left a pause long enough for that to land.

"I'm getting forgetful in my old age."

She did not put the bottle away. She set it beside her own cup, within easy reach, and leaned her forearms on the bar, left over right. The lamp threw her shadow long across the counter, and it nearly reached the cup at the far end.

"Well, then," Maren said. "You're down here, I'm down here, and the fire's not out yet. If you want to talk, I'm a fair listener. If you'd rather not, I'm a fair hand at silence too." The corner of her mouth moved. "The Kingsguard taught me both. Mostly the second."

**Traveler** (turn 15):
*I take a sip of the dark drink. It's surprisingly smooth.* "Kingsguard, huh? You don't look like much of a soldier, Maren." *I gesture vaguely at her apron and the bar around us.*

**Maren** (turn 16):
Maren looked down at herself: the apron, the rolled sleeves, the rag tucked at her string. She considered the evidence with the gravity of a magistrate.

"No," she agreed. "I do not suppose I do."

She lifted her cup with her left hand and took another swallow. Her eyes went briefly to the Traveler's cup, to the dark liquid in it, and she gave a small nod of approval, as though a guest had passed a test they had not known they were taking.

"Go slowly with that. It is smooth going down and it keeps its opinions for the morning. Rather like the bed."

She set her cup on the wood.

"I was not much of a soldier. I was a quartermaster. Five years. There is a difference, though the sergeants did not always think so, and the men who were hungry never did." She turned the silver ring on her thumb, once, a slow habitual quarter-turn. "A soldier's work is to stand in a line and be brave. A quartermaster's work is to make certain the line has boots to stand in, bread in its belly, and enough arrows that bravery is not the only thing it has to throw."

The fire settled in the hearth with a soft collapse of embers. Maren waited for it to finish.

"They say an army marches on its stomach. Somebody has to count the stomachs." A pause. "And the boots. And the barrels, and the horseshoes, and the blankets that went missing between one camp and the next and turned up, oddly enough, on the backs of a lieutenant's cousins." The corner of her mouth moved. "That is where I learned my letters and my sums. And where I learned that a ledger will tell you more about a man than his face ever will. Faces lie. Numbers only sulk."

She gestured, left-handed, at the common room around them: the empty tables, the chairs turned up on two of them, the long row of casks behind her with their chalked tallies, the key hooks with their labels.

"So you see, I did not leave the work behind. I only moved it somewhere with a better roof. Twelve rooms, forty seats, three staff, and a cook who must be managed like a supply line through hostile country." She glanced toward the kitchen door. "Tavern-keeping is quartermastering with better ale and fewer men trying to stab you. Most nights."

She flexed her right hand without seeming to notice she was doing it. She opened and closed it, slow, and the fingers did not quite close as tight as they should have.

"The Guard did leave me a keepsake, mind." She held up the wrist, turned it once in the lamplight, and lowered it again. "A supply wagon on a mountain road, a wheel that had been promised to me as sound, and a very stubborn mule. The mule won. I do not say that to many people. It is bad for the reputation to have been beaten by a mule." She considered that. "It was a very large mule."

She picked up the dark bottle, looked at it, and did not pour. She set it back down.

"I do not speak of it often, Traveler. It was a long while ago, and it was not very interesting, and nobody sings songs about the woman who counted the tent pegs." Her gaze came up, level and steady, and held. "But I will tell you the one thing it taught me worth keeping. When a man sends a gift he did not need to send, and asks a question he did not need to ask, and then takes a room he did not need to take, he is not being friendly. He is taking inventory."

Above them, the board on the right side of the landing gave a single long creak and went silent.

Maren did not look up this time.

"And I have always found," she said mildly, turning her cup a quarter turn on the wood, "that it is wise to know what is in your own stores before somebody else comes to count them for you."

**Traveler** (turn 17):
*I listen, completely engrossed, occasionally nodding. The creak from above makes me flinch slightly, but Maren's calm expression keeps me from reacting too strongly. I take another sip of the drink, letting her words sink in.* "He's not getting his hands on this, then." *I pat the mysterious package beside my feet.*

**Maren** (turn 18):
Maren did not look at the pack when it was patted. She looked at the Traveler's hand instead, and at the way it stayed resting there a moment after the pat was done.

"Not in my house, he is not," she said.

She said it the way she said the price of the ale: plainly, without any weight on it, as though it were simply the sort of thing that was true. Then she picked up her rag, found nothing that needed wiping, and folded it into a smaller square.

"I will say this once, Traveler, and then I will leave it be." The contractions had gone out of her voice. "I do not know what you are carrying. I do not wish to know. But I know that Lord Havel does not know either, and that is what troubles him. A man like that can bear to be refused. What he cannot bear is to be left out."

She set the folded rag down, square to the edge of the bar.
